newsitem.title: USA: Southeastern utilities stung hard by Fran.
newsitem.headline: Southeastern utilities stung hard by Fran.

text.p: At least four million residents of the battered U.S. southeast were without electricity Friday as crews struggled to untangle the trees, power lines, and debris left by Hurricane Fran.
"We're still assessing damage...the whole region is pretty messed up," said Rick Zuercher, a spokesman for Duke Power Co in Charlotte, N.C.
Hardest hit was Carolina Power & Light Co, which caught the full fury of the storm when it roared ashore late Thursday near Cape Fear, N.C., with winds up to 120 mph.
"This was a direct hit on our service area," said Carolina Power spokeman Mike Hughes.
"We have 670,000 customers without power out of a customer base of 1.1 million. That's nearly two-thirds of our customers, the vast majority of them in North Carolina."
Customers are measured by the number of electricity meters in a utility's service territory. There are typically three to four residents for every meter.
Fran, though downgraded early Friday to a tropical storm, tore a wide swath through the South on its north-northwesterly course.
Duke Power reported 377,000 of its 1.8 million customers in the central and western Carolinas had lost electricity.
To the north, Virginia Power Co, a subsidiary of Dominion Resources Inc, put the toll at 379,000 customers, adding "This may be the largest outage in the company's history."
Damage estimates were hard to come by.
Carolina Power, even before the storm struck, was predicting they would not know the extent of damage to their system until sometime Saturday.
The company, based in Raleigh, N.C., put the cost of Hurricane Bertha, a far less powerful storm that brushed along the North Carolina coast in July, at $8 to $10 million.
Hughes confirmed Fran caused "significant damage" to their transmission lines, the high-voltage lines linking generating facilities to local distribution lines.
"This is going to prolong recovery efforts," he said.
Local flooding and roadways littered with downed trees also were hampering the recovery effort.
Utility officials predict it could take at least a week to hook everyone back up to the grid, but that the majority of residents should have power again within the next two days.
To speed the work, power companies across the South are dispatching emergency crews to help their battered neighbours.
"It's a gentleman's agreement among the utilities. You never know when it might be your turn to need the help," said South Carolina Electric & Gas Co (SCE&G) spokesman Roger Schrumm.
Schrumm said their service territory, in southern and central South Carolina, had escaped Fran relatively unscathed, losing just 24,000 customers.

But it was a near miss. Earlier this week forecasters were predicting Fran would hit Charleston, S.C., cutting right through the heart of SCE&G's territory and raising fears of a repeat of Hurricane Hugo in 1989.
Damage from Hurricane Hugo, at $7 billion the second costliest storm in U.S. history, cost SCE&G about $53 million.
